Iwashitsunoo.note: Iwashitsunoo is generated from Kagutsuchi's blood.

Iwasu-hime.note: Rock-and-earth deity jointly generated by the pair.

Iwatsuchi-biko.note: Rock-and-earth deity jointly generated by the pair.

Iwatsutsunome.note: Iwatsutsunome appears in the genealogy generated from Kagutsuchi's blood.

Iwatsutsunoo.note: Arises from the blood shed when Izanagi kills Kagutsuchi.

Izuna Gongen.note: Fox-like izuna familiars serve or accompany this syncretic mountain deity.

Izunome.note: Emerges to rectify the evil generated by Izanagi's pollution.

Jadokuke-shin.note: Later Gion commentators sometimes equate Orochi with this poisonous-serpent deity.

Jimmu.note: Amaterasu is Jimmu’s divine ancestress through Ninigi’s descendant line.
Toyotama-hime is Jimmu's paternal grandmother through Ugayafukiaezu.

Jiten.note: The earth goddess physically supports Bishamonten in the Tōbatsu iconographic form.
Jiten.source: Medieval East Asian and Japanese iconography

Jurōjin.myth: Seven Gods aboard the treasure ship
Jurōjin.note: They jointly appear in the stabilized Seven Gods of Fortune roster, prints, and pilgrimage circuits.
Jurōjin and Bishamonten belong to the standard Japanese Seven Lucky Gods.

Jurōjin.myth: Voyage of the Seven Lucky Gods
Jurōjin.note: Daikokuten voyages and bears gifts with Jurōjin aboard the treasure ship.
Ebisu and Jurōjin jointly belong to the standard Seven Lucky Gods.

Kaguya-hime.note: Their identities competed or overlapped as female manifestations of Fuji and Sengen.

Kamimusubi.note: Kamimusubi sends Kisagaihime and Umugihime to restore the murdered Ōnamuji.
Kamimusubi gathers seeds arising from Ōgetsuhime’s corpse after Susanoo kills her.

Kamo Taketsunumi.note: Kamo Wakeikazuchi is the maternal grandson of Kamo Taketsunumi.

Kamo Wakeikazuchi.note: Honoikazuchi fathers Kamo Wakeikazuchi through Tamayorihime.

Kamu-Naobi.note: Emerges to rectify the evil generated by Izanagi's pollution.

Kamu-Ōichihime.note: Daughter of Ōyamatsumi and Susanoo’s consort, mothering Ōtoshi and Ukanomitama.

Kamuyatatehime.note: Through identification with Kotoshironushi, Ebisu is treated as Kamuyatatehime’s son.
She is Ōkuninushi’s consort and the mother of Kotoshironushi.

Kanayamabiko.note: Kanayamabiko arises from Izanami's vomit after Kagutsuchi burns her.

Kanayamabime.note: Kanayamabime arises from Izanami's vomit after Kagutsuchi burns her.

Kanayamahiko.myth: Gods born during Izanami's fatal illness
Kanayamahiko.note: Born from Izanami's vomit after Kagutsuchi burns her.
Kanayamahiko arises from Izanami's vomit during Kagutsuchi's delivery.

Kanayamahime.myth: Gods born during Izanami's fatal illness
Kanayamahime.note: Born from Izanami's vomit after Kagutsuchi burns her.

Kannon.note: Hōgonji tradition says Gyōki installed images of Benzaiten and Thousand-Armed Kannon together.
Kurama tradition joins Kannon’s compassion with Bishamonten’s state-protective power.
Kannon and Bishamonten are aspects of Kurama’s modern triune Sonten.
Some local and textual honji systems identify Kannon as Inari's Buddhist original ground.

Kannon.myth: Kannon intervenes in Buddhist fox narratives
Kannon.note: Kannon sometimes reveals or heals fox-related affliction and supplies karmic efficacy.

Karai Kaki Dokuō.note: Tenjin’s third divine messenger causes the palace lightning strike on his behalf.

Kasuga Daimyōjin.note: Hachiman, Kasuga, and Amaterasu jointly appear in the Sanja takusen oracle scheme.
A messenger of Kasuga obtains tide jewels from Sāgara’s dragon palace.
Takemikazuchi becomes both an individual member and an aspect of the collective Kasuga deity.

Kayanohime.note: Field or moor deity jointly generated by the pair.

Kazamotsuwake-no-oshi-o.note: Jointly generated by Izanagi and Izanami.

Kichijō-nyo.note: Kitano enshrines Kichijō-nyo as Michizane’s principal wife.

Kichijōten.note: Kichijōten sometimes joins Daikokuten in early variant rosters of the fortune gods.
Kichijōten occasionally appears with Ebisu in variant Lucky Gods memberships.

Kimata-no-kami.note: Kimata-no-kami is the child of Ōkuninushi and Yakamihime.

Kisagaihime.note: She prepares shell substance used to restore Ōnamuji after his fiery death.

Kisshōten.myth: Prosperity goddesses in the Golden Light Sūtra
Kisshōten.note: They appear separately in the scripture, and their prosperity functions later overlap without explicit identification.
One East Asian Buddhist tradition presents Kisshōten as Bishamonten’s sister.
Another East Asian Buddhist tradition presents Kisshōten as Bishamonten’s wife.
Bishamonten and Kisshōten appear together as associated fortune deities and in Japanese triads.
Kisshōten sometimes joins Bishamonten by replacing a standard Seven Lucky Gods member.

Konpira.note: Some regional explanations exempt Ebisu and Konpira from the gods’ journey to Izumo.

Kotoshironushi.note: Kotoshironushi accepts the land-transfer demand conveyed by Amaterasu’s heavenly envoys.
Fishing and coastal associations led many shrines to identify Kotoshironushi with Ebisu.
Kotoshironushi is Ōkuninushi’s son by Kamuyatatehime.
Ōkuninushi refers surrender to Kotoshironushi, who counsels acceptance.
Takemikazuchi’s demand is referred to Kotoshironushi, who consents to the transfer and withdraws.

Kuebiko.note: Kuebiko identifies the tiny arriving deity whom the assembled gods cannot recognize.

Kukunochi.note: Tree deity jointly generated by the pair.

Kumano Gongen.note: Kumano Gongen assists Raikō’s expedition against Shuten-dōji and his oni followers.

Kumano Ōkami Kushimikenu-no-Mikoto.note: An Izumo tradition identifies the Kumano deity with Susanoo, though details remain debated.

Kumanokusubi.note: Amaterasu claims Kumanokusubi as one of her five sons.
Generated from Amaterasu’s chewing of Susanoo’s sword; ownership and parentage are disputed.

Kumbhakarṇa.note: Kubera is the half-brother of Kumbhakarṇa in Hindu genealogy.

Kuni-no-Tokotachi.note: A variant genealogy places Kuni-no-Tokotachi at the head of Izanagi's line.

Kuni-no-mihashira.note: Later Tatsuta tradition identifies a wind deity with the August Pillar of the Land.

Kuramitsuha.note: Arises through Izanagi's killing and dismemberment of Kagutsuchi.
Kuramitsuha is generated from Kagutsuchi's blood.

Kuraokami.note: Arises through Izanagi's killing and dismemberment of Kagutsuchi.
Kuraokami is generated from Kagutsuchi's blood.

Kurayamatsumi.note: Kurayamatsumi emerges from Kagutsuchi's genital or hidden region.
A dark-mountain deity arises in a variant division of Kagutsuchi.

Kuroikazuchi.note: One of eight thunder deities inhabiting or born within Izanami's corpse.

Kushinadahime.note: The main Nihon shoki genealogy identifies Kushinadahime as Ōnamuchi’s mother.
Susanoo saves her from becoming Orochi’s eighth annual victim.
Susanoo transforms her into a comb and carries her in his hair.
She is Susanoo’s principal classical spouse and shares his palace at Suga.
Orochi is expected to consume her, but Susanoo transforms and hides her.

Kōra Daimyōjin.note: Kōra is represented as a subordinate or associated deity within Hachiman shrine complexes.

Maheśvara.note: Tenjin’s Daijizai-ten title invokes Maheśvara, though no simple identity is established.

Mahāvairocana.note: Esoteric systems treat both deities as dual manifestations of Dainichi.

Maitreya.note: Hachiman orders or supports Miroku-ji, institutionally coupling his worship with Maitreya.

Mañjuśrī.note: Mañjuśrī teaches in Sāgara’s palace; the link applies through later identification.

Mikahayahi.note: Arises from the blood shed when Izanagi kills Kagutsuchi.
Mikahayahi is generated from Kagutsuchi's blood.
Mikahayahi and Takemikazuchi are co-generated from blood on Izanagi’s sword.
One genealogy makes Mikahayahi Takemikazuchi’s grandparent through Hihayahi.
Takemikazuchi descends from Mikahayahi through the Hihayahi lineage.

Miketsu-no-kami.note: Homophonic exegesis reinterpreted the food deity’s name as “three fox kami.”

Minamoto no Raikō.note: Raikō decapitates Shuten-dōji and defeats his oni followers after intoxicating them.

Miroku.note: Emperor Ichijō, identified with Miroku, stands within the order opposing Shuten-dōji.

Mitsuhanome.myth: Gods born during Izanami's fatal illness
Mitsuhanome.note: Born from Izanami's urine during her fatal illness.
Mitsuhanome arises from Izanami's urine during Kagutsuchi-caused illness.

Mizuhanome.note: The water deity is generated or appointed to subdue the dangerous fire-child.

Momotarō.note: Momotarō invades Onigashima, defeats its oni, and returns with their treasure.

Monju.myth: Monju manifests as Inari and Celestial Fox divinities
Monju.note: Medieval ritual texts describe Inari and related fox divinities as Monju's temporary manifestation.

Monju.myth: Monju manifests as Inari and Celestial Fox divinities
Monju.note: A secret ritual complex identifies Inari-related fox divinities as manifestations of Monju.

Munakata Three Goddesses.note: They are identified with Hime Ōkami and thus share Hachiman's Usa sanctuary.
Munakata Three Goddesses.source: Hachiman gudōkun and later shrine traditions

Mutō Tennō.note: The preserved fragment has Mutō identify himself as Susanoo; later traditions vary.

Muzan.myth: Creation of oni through Muzan’s blood
Muzan.note: Muzan’s blood transforms humans into cannibalistic, regenerative oni.

Myōbu Tatsugitsune.myth: Fox spirit receives a Buddhist original ground
Myōbu Tatsugitsune.note: A fox spirit is interpreted through honji-suijaku and assigned Buddhist efficacy.

Māra.note: Medieval doctrine classifies tengu among māra's obstructive powers or as their agents.

Nakatsutsu-no-o.note: Arises alongside the Watatsumi triad during Izanagi’s washing.

Nakatsuwatatsumi.note: Born while Izanagi bathes at the middle depth.

Nakazutsunoo.note: Born during Izanagi's bath and identified as a Sumiyoshi god.

Nakisawame.note: Nakisawame is born from Izanagi's tears before he kills Kagutsuchi.

Nakizawame.note: Nakizawame is born from Izanagi's tears while he mourns Izanami.

Nalakūbara.note: Nalakūbara is presented as Vaiśravaṇa’s son or princely attendant.

Namazu.note: Takemikazuchi restrains the earthquake-causing catfish with the keystone and sometimes punishes or negotiates with it.

Naruikazuchi.note: One of eight thunder deities inhabiting or born within Izanami's corpse.

Nesaku.note: Arises from the blood shed when Izanagi kills Kagutsuchi.
Nesaku is generated from Kagutsuchi's blood upon Izanagi's sword.

Ninigi.note: Ninigi is Amaterasu’s grandson through Ame no Oshihomimi.
Amaterasu gives Ninigi sacred objects, including the mirror, and authority to descend.
Uzume accompanies Ninigi, obeys his orders, and secures marine allegiance.
She becomes Ninigi’s wife after he encounters her at Cape Kasasa.
After Ninigi questions her pregnancy, she proves his paternity through a fiery childbirth ordeal.
She refuses to speak to Ninigi after his accusation; he laments in song.
Ninigi receives the right to rule after Ōkuninushi transfers the terrestrial realm.

Ninigi no Mikoto.note: Sarutahiko offers his service and guides Ninigi's descent to earth.
Sarutahiko waits at the crossroads to guide Ninigi's descending procession.
Ninigi directs Uzume to escort Sarutahiko and bear his name in service.

Nunakawahime.note: Ōkuninushi courts her through antiphonal songs, and she accepts his visit.

Okame.note: Later art and popular religion identify Uzume with the comic auspicious female figure.
Okame.source: Early-modern masks; modern art and religion

Okitama no kami.note: Medieval Ise materials present Okitama as Sarutahiko's manifestation or functional continuation.
Some medieval Ise genealogical versions make Okitama a descendant of Sarutahiko.

Omoikane.note: Omoikane devises the ritual plan that draws Amaterasu from seclusion.
Omoikane later advises the heavenly rulers concerning divine policy.
Uzume performs within the cave-opening strategy devised by Omoikane.

Orpheus.myth: Orphic retelling of the Yomi descent
Orpheus.note: Fried explicitly recasts Izanagi through the parallel with Orpheus.

Osusuki.note: Inari accepts the benevolent male white fox as a retainer and names him Osusuki.

Otohime.note: Modern Urashima retellings commonly make Otohime the Dragon King’s daughter.
Modern popular writing sometimes equates Toyotama-hime with the Dragon Palace princess Otohime.

Pulastya.note: Kubera or Vaiśravaṇa is presented as Pulastya’s grandson.

Ranba.note: Ranba flanks or supports Bishamonten as a female demon attendant.

Sada no Ōkami.note: Hirata-influenced scholarship and Sada Shrine doctrine identify Sada with Sarutahiko.
Sada no Ōkami.source: Hirata writings and Sada Shrine doctrine

Sakuikazuchi.note: One of eight thunder deities inhabiting or born within Izanami's corpse.

Sarasvant.note: Sarasvatī and her male counterpart Sarasvant are invoked in the same hymn.

Seven unnamed divine daughters.myth: Annual consumption of the divine daughters
Seven unnamed divine daughters.note: Orochi eats one unnamed daughter of Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi each year.

Shi-no-Ōkami.note: Shi is an auxiliary member of the later fivefold Fushimi Inari.

Shigiyamatsumi.note: Shigiyamatsumi emerges from Kagutsuchi's left hand.

Shinatsuhiko.note: Wind deity jointly generated by the pair.

Shiotsuchi-no-oji.myth: Hoori journeys to the Sea-God’s palace
Shiotsuchi-no-oji.note: Shiotsuchi directs or transports Hoori into the Sea-God’s realm.

Shitateruhime.note: Shitateruhime is Ōkuninushi’s daughter by Takiribime.

Shukongōjin.note: Shukongōjin guides Dōken through the otherworld toward Tenjin’s celestial court.

Shōgun Jizō.note: Atago's Buddhist-kami complex associated Kagutsuchi's later cult setting with Shōgun Jizō.
Tengu traditions coexist with Shōgun Jizō, mountain asceticism, and fire protection at Atago.

Shōjō.note: Shōjō sometimes joins Bishamonten by replacing a standard Seven Lucky Gods member.
Shōjō sometimes joins Daikokuten in early variant rosters of the fortune gods.
Shōjō occasionally appears with Ebisu in variant Lucky Gods memberships.

Sokotsutsu-no-o.note: Arises alongside the Watatsumi triad during Izanagi’s washing.

Sokotsuwatatsumi.note: Born while Izanagi bathes at the bottom depth.

Sokozutsunoo.note: Born during Izanagi's bath and identified as a Sumiyoshi god.

Sukunabikona.note: Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku secondarily inherits Sukunabikona’s assistance in developing the land.
The two gods complete the land and develop healing, agriculture, and magic.
Ōnamuchi retains excrement while Sukunabikona carries clay until both drop their burdens.

Sumiyoshi.myth: Divine defense against the Mongol invasions
Sumiyoshi.note: Fūjin and Sumiyoshi act in parallel within the multi-shrine defense sequence.

Sumiyoshi Myōjin.note: Sumiyoshi guides or equips Raikō’s party in its campaign against the oni.

Sumiyoshi deities.note: Hachiman and the Sumiyoshi deities receive offerings as parallel national protectors.

Suseribime.note: Daikoku secondarily inherits Ōkuninushi’s marriage to Suseribime and their escape.
She marries Ōnamuji and becomes his principal wife.
She supplies protective scarves and helps Ōnamuji survive Susanoo’s ordeals.
Suseribime is Susanoo’s daughter and later Ōkuninushi’s wife.
Suseribime secretly helps Ōkuninushi survive Susanoo’s trials and escape his realm.

Suwa.myth: Divine defense against the Mongol invasions
Suwa.note: Fūjin and Suwa act in parallel within the multi-shrine defense sequence.

Sāgara Ryūō.note: Later Japanese thought equates this Buddhist ocean dragon king with the sea-palace sovereign.

Sāgara’s dragon daughter.note: She is Sāgara’s daughter; the relation applies through syncretic identification.

Tagitsuhime.note: Amaterasu generates her by chewing Susanoo’s sword during their pledge.
She became one of Enoshima Shrine’s official kami replacing or institutionally translating Benzaiten after separation.
Generated when Susanoo chews Amaterasu’s jewels; ownership and parentage vary by account.

Tagorihime.note: Amaterasu generates her by chewing Susanoo’s sword during their pledge.
She became one of Enoshima Shrine’s official kami replacing or institutionally translating Benzaiten after separation.
Generated when Susanoo chews Amaterasu’s jewels; ownership and parentage vary by account.

Takagi.note: Takagi participates with Amaterasu in selecting and commissioning Takemikazuchi as heavenly envoy.

Takagi no kami.note: He and Amaterasu commission Uzume to investigate the radiant terrestrial deity.

Takamimusubi.note: Takamimusubi shares heavenly authority with Amaterasu in pacification and descent.
Uzume obeys the heavenly mandate to question Sarutahiko at the crossroads.
Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku inherits the surrender of the land under heavenly authority.
Takamimusubi identifies Sukunabikona as his child and assigns him to aid Ōnamuchi.
Takamimusubi joins the heavenly decision to claim and pacify Ōkuninushi’s realm.
The possessing Moon God calls Takamimusubi his ancestor.

Takaokami.note: Takaokami is one of three beings produced from Kagutsuchi's divided body.

Takehazuchi.myth: Suppression of the hostile star deity
Takehazuchi.note: Takehazuchi receives the decisive star-subduing role within an account connected to Takemikazuchi’s mission.

Takeminakata.note: Takeminakata resists Amaterasu’s land-transfer program and loses to Takemikazuchi.
Through Kotoshironushi, Ebisu is treated as sibling of Ōkuninushi’s other son Takeminakata.
Takeminakata is abruptly introduced as Ōkuninushi’s son during the land transfer.
Takemikazuchi transforms his arm, crushes and throws Takeminakata, then forces his submission at Suwa.

Takiribime.note: She bears Ōkuninushi’s children Ajisukitakahikone and Takahime.

Tamanooya.note: Tamanooya produces the jewel string displayed during Amaterasu’s rescue.

Tamanoya.note: Tamanoya supplies jeweled strings for the ritual in which Uzume performs.

Tamatori.note: Tamatori takes the precious pearl from the Dragon Palace.
The Dragon King and his marine court pursue Tamatori through the sea.

Tamayori-hime.note: Tamayori-hime is the Sea-God’s younger daughter.
Toyotama-hime sends her sister to rear Ugayafukiaezu and convey a song to Hoori.

Tamayorihime.note: Honoikazuchi becomes a red arrow beside Tamayorihime, who conceives their son.

Tanaka-no-Ōkami.note: Tanaka is an auxiliary member of the later fivefold Fushimi Inari.

Tenazuchi.note: Susanoo questions her family, negotiates for her daughter, and directs the sake preparations.

Tenazuchi.myth: Annual consumption of the divine daughters
Tenazuchi.note: Orochi annually consumes her daughters, leaving only the final threatened child.
She participates in preparing the liquor and trap used against Orochi.

The Seven Mothers.note: Mahākāla governs, subdues, or converts the Mothers and their dangerous appetites.

The Twenty-Eight Attendants.note: They appear before Tenjin’s manifestation, without direct conversation between them.

The White Hare of Inaba.myth: Healing the White Hare of Inaba
The White Hare of Inaba.note: Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku secondarily inherits the episode of healing the injured hare.

Thousand-Armed Kannon.note: Fūjin appears as a guardian attendant protecting Kannon and the Dharma.
Raijin appears as a guardian protecting Kannon and the Dharma.

Torinarumi.note: Torinarumi is the child of Ōkuninushi and Totori-no-kami.

Totori-no-kami.note: Totori-no-kami is Ōkuninushi’s consort and Torinarumi’s mother.

Toyamatsumi.note: Toyamatsumi emerges from Kagutsuchi's right foot.

Toyouke.note: Exegetical traditions equate Toyouke with Ukanomitama, though their institutions remain distinct.

Toyouke Ōmikami.note: Amaterasu requests Toyouke from Tanba to provide her sacred food.

Toyoukehime.note: Izanami is Toyoukehime's grandmother through Wakumusubi.

Tsuchiikazuchi.note: One of eight thunder deities inhabiting or born within Izanami's corpse.

Tsumatsuhime.note: She carries out responsibility for spreading useful trees generated by Susanoo.

Uga Benzaiten.note: Uga Benzaiten shares Inari's medieval fertility, food, serpent, jewel, and wish-granting complexes.

Ugajin.note: Ugajin is bodily and ritually fused with Benzaiten in medieval esoteric images and rites.
Ugajin.source: Medieval Uga Benzaiten texts and images

Ugajin.note: Ugajin is linked with Inari through food, fertility, serpent, jewel, and prosperity symbolism.

Ugayafukiaezu.note: Ugayafukiaezu is the Sea-God’s grandson through Toyotama-hime.

Ugayafukiaezu.myth: Birth in the unfinished shore hut
Ugayafukiaezu.note: Toyotama-hime gives birth to him, leaves him ashore, and arranges his care.

Uhō Dōji.note: Regional Ise tradition links the rain-treasure child’s esoteric imagery with Amaterasu.

Ukanomitama.note: Ukanomitama is Susanoo’s child through Kamu-Ōichihime.

Ukanomitama-no-kami.note: Foxes attend Ukanomitama where later shrine theology identifies the grain kami with Inari.

Ukemochi.note: Tsukuyomi rejects Ukemochi’s mouth-produced feast and kills her with a sword.

Ukemochi-no-kami.note: Later learned and cultic traditions compare or equate this food deity with Ukanomitama and Inari.
Foxes serve the Inari complex at shrines identifying or jointly worshipping Ukemochi.

Umugihime.note: She mixes the restorative remedy with maternal milk and revives Ōnamuji.

Unborn daughter of Inada-no-Miyanushi-Su.myth: Aki river and unborn child variant
Unborn daughter of Inada-no-Miyanushi-Su.note: Orochi approaches to consume her at birth but is diverted and killed.

Urashima Tarō.note: Later folklore places Urashima in Ryūjin’s palace, unlike the earliest versions.

Uwatsutsu-no-o.note: Arises alongside the Watatsumi triad during Izanagi’s washing.

Uwatsuwatatsumi.note: Born while Izanagi bathes at the water's surface.

Uwazutsunoo.note: Born during Izanagi's bath and identified as a Sumiyoshi god.

Vairocana.note: Vairocana assumes or deploys Mahākāla’s form to restrain murderous demonesses.
Hachiman promises successful casting and ceremonially visits the Great Buddha in 749.

Vibhīṣaṇa.note: Kubera is the half-brother of Vibhīṣaṇa in Hindu genealogy.

Virūpākṣa.note: Virūpākṣa guards the west while Vaiśravaṇa jointly guards the north.

Virūḍhaka.note: Virūḍhaka guards the south while Vaiśravaṇa jointly guards the north.

Viśravas.note: Kubera or Vaiśravaṇa is genealogically presented as the son of Viśravas.

Wakahirume.myth: Death in the heavenly weaving hall
Wakahirume.note: A variant makes Wakahirume the weaver fatally injured by Susanoo’s horse.

Wakaikazuchi.note: One of eight thunder deities inhabiting or born within Izanami's corpse.

Wakumusubi.myth: Gods born during Izanami's fatal illness
Wakumusubi.note: Born from Izanami's urine during her fatal illness.
Wakumusubi is the child of Kagutsuchi and Haniyamahime.
Wakumusubi instead arises from Izanami's urine after Kagutsuchi's burning birth.

Watanabe no Tsuna.note: Tsuna fights a disguised oni and cuts off its arm.

Yahashira-no-Mikogami.note: The collective is worshiped with Susanoo and Kushiinadahime in Yasaka’s modern sanctuary.

Yakamihime.note: She chooses Ōnamuji over the eighty brothers and bears his child.

Yamatohime no Mikoto.note: Yamatohime carries Amaterasu’s cult and receives her oracle choosing Ise.

Yaoyorozu-no-kami.note: The heavenly gods collectively judge Susanoo for his transgressions.
They impose fines, bodily penalties in variants, and expel Susanoo.

Yashimajinumi.note: Yashimajinumi begins the ancestral chain connecting Ōkuninushi to Susanoo.
Yashimajinumi is the child of Susanoo and Kushinadahime.

Yaso-Magatsuhi.note: Emerges from the pollution accumulated by Izanagi in Yomi.

Yasogami.note: Ōnamuji is the youngest member of the company of eighty brothers.
The brothers murder Ōnamuji with a fiery rock and later a split tree.
After escaping Susanoo, Ōkuninushi expels or subdues his hostile brothers.

Yomotsu-shikome.note: Izanami sends the pursuer after Izanagi, who delays it with grapes and bamboo shoots.

Zaō Bosatsu.note: Zaō mediates Dōken’s encounter with Tenjin as a heavenly sovereign.

Zennishi Dōji.note: Japanese devotional triads sometimes represent Zennishi Dōji as Bishamonten’s son.
Zennishi Dōji also appears as Bishamonten’s youthful attendant.

field mouse.note: The speaking mouse reveals a refuge and retrieves Susanoo’s arrow.

flesh- and blood-eating spirits.note: Mahākāla travels nocturnally with a host consuming human flesh and vital essence.

flesh-eating female spirits.note: In Mahākāla form, he stops the spirits killing humans and redirects them to Dharma service.

giant centipede of Mount Mikami.note: The centipede attacks the aquatic palace until Hidesato destroys it.

hare of Inaba.note: Ōnamuji heals the flayed hare with fresh water and cattail pollen.
The healed hare prophesies that Yakamihime will choose Ōnamuji.

jellyfish.note: The Dragon King sends a jellyfish to obtain a monkey’s liver.

monkey.note: The monkey deceives the Dragon King’s jellyfish and avoids losing its liver.

the Buddha.note: Early Buddhist discourse could classify the Buddha as a foreign or neighboring kami.

the Four Heavenly Kings.myth: Protectors in the Golden Light Sūtra
the Four Heavenly Kings.note: They appear alongside her as parallel royal and Dharma protectors without a discrete personal encounter.

the Twenty-Eight Attendants.note: Fūjin appears beside the attendants, often outside their unstable nominal list.
Raijin appears beside the attendants, often outside their unstable nominal list.

the collective heavenly and earthly kami.note: Hachiman promises to lead the collective kami in completing the Great Buddha.

the collective heavenly deities.myth: Commission to consolidate the drifting land
the collective heavenly deities.note: They commission the pair, grant the jeweled spear, and diagnose the failed marriage.

the deities of Yomi.note: Izanami says she must consult them before she can return with Izanagi.

the eight mountain deities.myth: Mountain gods arise from Kagutsuchi's body
the eight mountain deities.note: They arise from pieces of Kagutsuchi dismembered by Izanagi.

the eight thunder deities.note: The eight thunders inhabit or are born within Izanami's corpse.
Izanami dispatches them after Izanagi, who drives the pursuing host away.

the gods.note: The gods assemble at Izumo to deliberate relationships under Ōkuninushi’s leadership.

yakṣas.note: Vaiśravaṇa rules and commands yakṣas as guardian of the northern quarter.

Ō-Magatsuhi.note: Emerges from the pollution accumulated by Izanagi in Yomi.

Ō-Naobi.note: Emerges to rectify the evil generated by Izanagi's pollution.

Ōgetsuhime.note: Later learned and cultic traditions compare or equate this food deity with Ukanomitama and Inari.
Food deity jointly generated by the pair.
Susanoo kills her after mistaking her bodily production of food for pollution.

Ōikazuchi.note: One of eight thunder deities inhabiting or born within Izanami's corpse.

Ōkamuzumi.note: Three peaches repel Izanagi's pursuers, enabling his escape.
Izanagi names the peaches and commissions them to aid distressed living people.

Ōkoto-oshi-o.note: Jointly generated by Izanagi and Izanami.

Ōkuninushi’s mother.note: His mother obtains divine aid, revives him again, and directs his escape.

Ōmiyame-no-kami.note: Medieval and modern shrine theology sometimes equates these female court-service kami.

Ōmiyanome.note: Ōmiyanome shares Fushimi's principal seats and later five-kami Inari collective.

Ōmononushi.myth: Miwa god appears in Daikoku form
Ōmononushi.note: The Miwa deity appears as Daikoku Tenshin, provides wood, and protects Hiei’s foundation.
The sea-arriving deity offers completion if Ōkuninushi worships him at Miwa.
One account calls Ōmononushi Ōnamuchi’s fortunate and wondrous soul-components.

Ōta-no-mikoto.note: Medieval Ise materials present Ōta as Sarutahiko's manifestation or functional continuation.
Some medieval Ise genealogical versions make Ōta a descendant of Sarutahiko.

Ōtohi-wake.note: Jointly generated by Izanagi and Izanami.

Ōtoshi.note: Ōtoshi and Ukanomitama are children of Susanoo and Kamu-Ōichihime.
Ōtoshi is Susanoo’s child through Kamu-Ōichihime.

Ōyabiko.note: Jointly generated by Izanagi and Izanami.

Ōyamatsumi.note: Ukanomitama descends from Ōyamatsumi through his daughter Kamu-Ōichihime.
Mountain deity jointly generated by the pair.
Ōyamatsumi is one of three beings produced from Kagutsuchi's divided body.
Mountain deities, including Ōyamatsumi, arise from Kagutsuchi's five portions.
She is his daughter; he arranges her marriage to Ninigi.
Ōyamatsumi is Susanoo’s affinal ancestor and father of his consort Kamu-Ōichihime.

Ōyatsuhime.note: She carries out responsibility for spreading useful trees generated by Susanoo.

Śiva.note: Mahākāla is a terrible black, temporal, and death-associated form of Śiva.
Daikokuten is presented as an emanation of Maheśvara.

Śākyamuni.myth: Vow to protect the Golden Light scripture
Śākyamuni.note: She appears before his assembly and vows to protect the scripture’s teachers, reciters, and hearers.
Some Kasuga interpretations identify Śākyamuni as Takemikazuchi’s Buddhist original ground.

Śākyamuni Buddha.note: Vaiśravaṇa attends the Buddha and promises to protect his teaching and community.
Vessavaṇa and the other Kings give the Buddha a protective recitation against hostile beings.
Nichiren argues that Hachiman is Śākyamuni's manifestation and protector of the Dharma.

Śūrpaṇakhā.note: Kubera is the half-brother of Śūrpaṇakhā in Hindu genealogy.
